nodes.label: KavitaClient (lib/src/api/kavita_client.dart)
nodes.rationale: Hand-written and wrapping only the endpoints the app uses; parsing in models.dart is defensive (?? defaults) because Kavita omits null fields. Two auth mechanisms coexist: JWT Bearer header for regular calls and the user's apiKey as a query param for image URLs, and image widgets get both because they cannot always send headers. Series listing is POST /api/Series/all-v2, which silently caps at the page size, so allSeriesForLibrary pages until a short page comes back — a single call would truncate a library at 100 series. It refreshes an expired JWT on a 401 and retries; a failure of the retried request is not a session failure.

nodes.label: LibraryTypeNaming / entity_naming.dart
nodes.rationale: Mirrors Kavita's EntityNamingService: a comic has issues where a manga has chapters, and a book library calls a volume a book at both levels. Never hardcode 'chapter' or 'volume' in a screen; get the type from libraryTypeProvider(libraryId), which falls back to manga while the library list is in flight so no screen waits on it. It names only what is numbered — a title never reaches the resume button, because free text stretches it across the hero and a Book library would do it every time. A special is known by its title alone and never numbered; a title is appended to the number, not swapped for it, and only when it says something the number does not.

nodes.label: MangaFormat and the PDF/EPUB split
nodes.rationale: PDFs read through the normal image reader: /api/Reader/image takes extractPdf, with which Kavita rasterises the PDF into one image per page; without it every page 404s. _readerImageQuery passes it unconditionally, harmless elsewhere since Kavita only reads the flag on its PDF/EPUB branch. Extraction happens on the first request and can take a while, so PageLoading shows the ordinary spinner and only after 1.8s and only for a PDF says what the server is doing. EPUB cannot: it is reflowable text, ReadingItemService.Extract does nothing for it, and it needs the /api/Book endpoints and a reader of its own with bookScrollId progress. Until then MangaFormat.isImageReadable keeps EPUB rows non-tappable and unsavable and the reader refuses them outright.

nodes.label: Kavita sentinel numbers (ParserConstants)
nodes.rationale: A volume with minNumber == -100000 holds the chapters belonging to no volume, +100000 holds the specials, and a chapter with -100000 is the placeholder for a volume with no chapter breakdown. Same magnitude, opposite signs — the sign is the whole distinction — so never compare on abs(), which silently files the specials volume under loose-leaf and makes isSpecials dead code. VolumeDto.isLooseLeaf / isSpecials / ChapterDto.isVolumePlaceholder exist so these never reach the UI as '-100000'. ChapterDto.sortOrder is Kavita's reading order and is not the order of the JSON array.

nodes.label: Chapter
nodes.rationale: The reading unit: the thing a row opens and the thing reading progress attaches to. Called an issue in a comic library and a book in a book library — always name it in the library type's own vocabulary, never as a bare 'chapter'. Avoid: episode, part, file.

nodes.label: Issue
nodes.rationale: What a chapter is called in a Comic or ComicVine library. Always written with the number sign — Issue #12.

nodes.label: Loose chapter
nodes.rationale: A chapter that belongs to no volume, listed under the library type's own chapter heading alongside the volumes. Avoid: orphan chapter, standalone chapter, loose-leaf chapter (that names the container, not the chapter).

nodes.label: Pseudo-volume
nodes.rationale: One of the two containers Kavita invents to hold what does not fit the numbering: the loose-leaf volume and the specials volume. Both carry a sentinel number and neither is ever shown as a volume. Neither is a place to hide a chapter: one filed under specials without isSpecial is still listed, and a special inside a numbered volume is filtered out of it so it does not appear twice. Avoid: virtual volume, fake volume, bucket.

nodes.label: Special
nodes.rationale: A chapter Kavita has flagged as a special: an extra, a one-shot, something outside the numbered run. Known by its title alone and never numbered. Avoid: extra, bonus, one-shot.

nodes.label: Storyline
nodes.rationale: The volumes and loose chapters of a series read as one ordered story. Only a storyline when the series actually has both, and only in a library type where it means something — an issue run is not a storyline and a book library has no chapter level. Kavita shows it for Manga and Image libraries; our series screen has sections rather than tabs, so the storyline is the header over volumes and loose chapters, and with only volumes it stays 'Tomes'. Avoid: timeline, reading order.

nodes.label: Volume
nodes.rationale: A numbered collection of chapters within a series. In a book library a volume is the book and has no chapters under it. Avoid: tome in English text, book except in a book library.

nodes.label: We do not generate a client
nodes.norm_label: we do not generate a client
nodes.rationale: Measured against 0.9.0.0: the spec describes 485 operations and 319 schemas while the app calls 22 paths and reads 6 of SeriesDto's 38 fields and 10 of ChapterDto's 81, so ~90% of a generated surface would be dead code. It is Swashbuckle output — required appears on 60 schemas, none a response type we read, and nullable:true marks reference types only, so every int, bool and DateTime is non-nullable and not required; a generator emits either models that crash on an unread series or models nullable everywhere, which nine hand-written classes already are. The declared security scheme (x-api-key header) is not what this app uses; there are zero operationIds; /api/Reader/image declares no content; all 485 operations declare exactly one response, 200, so nothing could feed ConnectionFailure. Every expensive fact came from Kavita's C# source, not the spec.

nodes.label: The OpenAPI spec as an oracle (openapi_contract_test)
nodes.norm_label: the openapi spec as an oracle (openapi_contract_test)
nodes.rationale: The defensive parsing swallows a mistyped key into a plausible default — json['format'] mistyped makes every EPUB row tappable, json['type'] makes a comic library say 'chapitre' — and neither throws nor fails another test. The test asserts each path and method exists, that every key models.dart reads exists and is typed compatibly with its cast, that no key read is deprecated (which flags ChapterDto.number and VolumeDto.number, hence minNumber), and that each hardcoded enum value matches x-enum-varnames. The field list is derived by reading models.dart, never listed — a list is where such a check rots. Enum values are looked up by value never by position, since SeriesSortField is one-based where the other three filter enums are zero-based. It deliberately does not assert required/nullable, response content types, or status codes. A missing spec fails the suite rather than skipping it.

nodes.label: We deliberately do not call /api/Series/series-detail
nodes.rationale: It returns the buckets ready-made but is documented as internal ('may change without hesitation') and its labels come pre-formatted in the server account's locale, which would fight our own fr/en. We take /api/Series/volumes and apply its rules ourselves.

nodes.label: DownloadsService and the meta.json-last invariant
nodes.rationale: Stores pages under <documents>/downloads/<chapterId>/, one extension-less file per page, and writes meta.json last — a chapter directory without one is a partial download and is deleted on the next scan(). DownloadsNotifier owns per-chapter CancelTokens; a cancelled or failed download leaves nothing behind. A save that waited on the first scan() must re-read state.value after the await, or a second pill tapped during that wait writes its own entry which the stale snapshot drops, leaving a download nothing tracks and a pill offering to start it again over the files being written. Progress is mirrored into each saved chapter's meta.json via recordProgress because the Downloads tab has to show it with no server; a chapter opened from that tab must open at its stored page, since opening at 0 posts that back and wipes the reader's place.

nodes.label: ImageCacheStore and its byte cap
nodes.rationale: Two stores must not be confused: saved chapters live in the documents directory, are chosen by the user and never evicted, while the image cache is cached_network_image's own store in the system cache directory and may be reclaimed by the OS (it outgrew the downloads three to one on a real device). Clearing the cache must never touch the documents directory. trim(maxBytes) deletes oldest-first because flutter_cache_manager only caps by number of objects, which says nothing about bytes; the sweep works on files directly, safe because the manager re-checks a file exists before serving its row. 'Oldest' is by write time, since atime is unreliable on Android. trim runs at startup, whenever the limit changes, and throttled via trimIfDue on every reader page turn.

nodes.label: readOverridesProvider — optimistic progress writes
nodes.rationale: seriesVolumesProvider lays the override over the fetch so the row redraws on the gesture rather than the round trip. Re-fetching would be worse than slow: the screen pattern-matches AsyncData, so any invalidate of volumesProvider drops the whole list to its skeleton. A refused write clears the override. The map is autoDispose and dies with the screen, so the next visit is the server's word; _open clears the chapter's override since reading is about to define progress properly. The hero's cover ring is series-wide and cannot be guessed from one chapter, so it re-fetches seriesProvider — flash-free, because the hero reads .value.

nodes.label: ThumbLoadQueue
nodes.rationale: Thumbnails do not load when built: the queue holds them 180ms, then fetches at most two at a time, nearest the current page first and only pages on screen — a flick through a 200-page chapter used to fire a request per thumbnail mounted. A failed thumbnail is marked done, never retried. The precache and the widget must ask for the same decode width, because ResizeImage puts it in the cache key: a mismatch precaches one image and displays another, and a decode a third of the drawn size is the blur the strip exists to avoid.

nodes.label: Image cache
nodes.rationale: The covers and pages kept on disk merely because they were looked at online. It fills on its own, is capped, and the OS may reclaim it. It is not the offline library and must never be counted as one. Avoid: downloads, offline storage.

nodes.label: Reading progress
nodes.rationale: How much has been read, counted in pages. It exists per chapter and per series, and the two answer different questions: finishing a volume leaves the next one untouched, so whether a series is under way is not what the chapter you would open next says. Avoid: completion, status, read state.

nodes.label: Saved chapter
nodes.rationale: A chapter whose pages are stored on the device because the user asked for them. Chosen deliberately, never evicted, readable with no server at all. This is what the Downloads tab counts. Avoid: download (that is the act of fetching one), cached chapter, offline chapter.

nodes.label: Chapter row swipes: leading = progress, trailing = destruction
nodes.norm_label: chapter row swipes: leading = progress, trailing = destruction
nodes.rationale: The two edges never mean the same kind of thing: leading marks read/unread in patraAccent, trailing removes the saved copy in patraDanger. markChapterRead posts to mark-multiple-read / mark-multiple-unread because there is no single-chapter unread endpoint and that pair takes one body shape for both directions. It needs the server, so the leading pane is gone offline; it does not need a readable format, since a file read elsewhere is exactly what one marks by hand. The stored copy's progress is mirrored alongside or the Downloads tab would disagree with no server to ask.

nodes.label: hasReadingProgress — the hero asks about the series
nodes.norm_label: hasreadingprogress — the hero asks about the series
nodes.rationale: Reading progress off the target chapter alone said 'Commencer la lecture' to someone halfway through a series, because finishing a volume leaves the next one untouched. Kavita's own web client asks the question of the series rather than the chapter; hasReadingProgress is that client's concept and appears nowhere in the API, so this mirrors a rule rather than reading a field.

nodes.label: Serialized progress posts and the last-page rule
nodes.norm_label: serialized progress posts and the last-page rule
nodes.rationale: Posts are serialized through a queue so a slow save cannot regress a later page, and the last page reports pages, not pages - 1, because Kavita only marks a chapter read when pagesRead >= pages. The initial page is saved on open, since onPageChanged never fires for it, and that initial save is deferred a frame because it is reached from build and writing to a provider while the tree is building is what Riverpod refuses outright.

nodes.label: _SqueezedByPane — a pane squeezes the row
nodes.rationale: Slidable uncovers a pane by translating its whole child, which carries the cover and title off the leading edge — the swipe hides the very thing it is about to act on. The wrapper works from inside that translation: it undoes it and hands the pane's edge the same width as padding, so the row keeps its origin and every part of itself and is merely narrower. Only the pane's own width is squeezed out; a drag that pulls further keeps the library's slide, which is where the over-drag gets its rubber band. Without it the title's left edge goes from 78pt to -16pt.

nodes.label: PatraFrond widget (lib/src/widgets/patra_frond.dart)
nodes.rationale: The mark itself, shared by the animation and the header, with geometry in the SVG's own 88x88 tile space so the Dart file, res/drawable/patra_mark.xml and the icon bitmaps can be read against one another. Sized by the mark, not the tile. Parchment (#E9E2D0) is private to the file and has no theme token: brand-mark-only, never in the UI.

nodes.label: LaunchAnimation and launch_composition.dart
nodes.rationale: LaunchStage is a pure function of authored time so the timeline can be read and pinned without a widget tree. Five beats over 7.8s transcribed beat for beat from the handoff's patra-launch.jsx; the numbers are the design's, not ours to round. A blade does not grow in place: it starts flat out at -72° for all five, swings to its angle and is drawn narrower while it travels (0.18 + 0.82·turn^0.8), which is what makes five identical sweeps read as pages rather than a flower opening. It wraps the whole app from MaterialApp.builder rather than being a route, because the last beat needs the frond flying and the app laid out underneath — which also means first requests are answered while the splash plays. A tap seeks to the last beat and lands in 500ms; MediaQuery.disableAnimations skips it outright; created once at app start, a resume is not a launch.

nodes.label: LaunchSlot registry (LaunchLogoSlot / LaunchWordmarkSlot)
nodes.rationale: The flight is aimed at measured slots, not at numbers, and looked up by render box rather than a global key handed down — two screens carry slots and a route transition can have both mounted for a frame, which one global key answers with a crash. The frond's bounds are flown onto the mark slot's rect, since the tile is larger than the mark. Everything is measured through the frame actually laid out (the one before the tick doing the measuring), so _painted keeps the last stage and its offsets come back off every rect; without those corrections the frond lands 18pt low and the wordmark 14pt low. The outro adapts to the screen it lands on, not to a flag: the presence of a slot is the question and the answer, so nothing asks whether a server is configured.

nodes.label: The palm frond mark and its two masters
nodes.norm_label: the palm frond mark and its two masters
nodes.rationale: Five-blade fan (patra-1024.png) and three-blade compact (patra-compact-1024.png). Below about 72px the five blades and their gaps each fall under two pixels and the fan closes into a blob, so every icon at or under 72px is rendered from the compact master. flutter_launcher_icons was removed because it rasterises one master to every size; ./tool/gen_app_icons.sh reads only from assets/icon/ so a fresh clone can regenerate, strips alpha for iOS and gives Android the platform's 22.7% corner.

nodes.label: Android adaptive icon (patra_mark.xml vector)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately not generated: a vector foreground cannot pixelate at any size and no generator can rewrite ic_launcher.xml with an inset that double-pads a vector already carrying padding. Transcribed from master/patra-frond.svg — five capsule blades at ±50°, ±26°, 0°, centre blade in the accent, accent stem below the pivot. Only the middle 66dp of the 108dp canvas is guaranteed visible, so the mark is scaled to 0.76 (bounding-box corner 32.1dp from centre, inside the 33dp radius) and the pivot drops to y=71.5 so the box is centred. Blade extremes come off cap centres grown by the radius, since a capsule has no corners. The mono variant lifts its parchment steps because a tinted line that faint disappears on some wallpapers — ordering carries the fan, not absolute values.

nodes.label: The OS launch screen is the ink and nothing else
nodes.norm_label: the os launch screen is the ink and nothing else
nodes.rationale: Centring the mark was right when Flutter's first frame was the finished app; now the app opens by growing the frond out of an empty screen, so a mark painted by the window would appear, vanish at Flutter's first frame and rebuild itself. What must be continuous from cold start is the ink, not the logo. On Android 12+ windowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon points at a deliberately transparent drawable, because the system always composites something and reaches for the launcher icon when the attribute is unset. iOS mirrors it and the LaunchImage imageset is deleted rather than left behind.

nodes.label: PatraWordmark lockup at two scales
nodes.rationale: One definition of the word, because the launch animation lands its own on the other two and drifted tracking would show at the one moment they are compared directly. The login masthead carries the same lockup at mark 40 × 24/22. Its gap is the one number that does not scale — 0.65em against the header's 0.81em — because spacing that reads as one lockup at 22pt opens into a gulf at 40pt: what is held constant is that mark and word read as one thing, not the ratio. The header draws the five-blade fan at 24pt, not the compact one: the mock's ~16pt three-blade mark was measured against a 17px wordmark, and at 22pt the same lockup gives a mark that reads as a plain arrow after two seconds of unfurling five blades.

nodes.label: The splash is outside every Material in the app
nodes.norm_label: the splash is outside every material in the app
nodes.rationale: Text there falls back to Flutter's error style and, since the wordmark's style sets no decoration, the leaking attribute is a yellow double underline. Material(type: transparency) supplies a real DefaultTextStyle; test/launch_animation_test.dart pins it because the symptom is easy to reintroduce and looks like a font problem rather than a missing ancestor.

nodes.label: ConnectionFailure classifier
nodes.rationale: Turns a thrown DioException into the few cases that change what someone would do next rather than printing a type, a URI and a socket error. Kavita answers every credential-side failure of /api/Account/login with a bare 401 in the server account's locale, so the six cannot be told apart and one message covers them, worded to stay true of a lockout. A 200 carrying someone else's HTML fails in the decode, which dio reports as unknown with no response attached, so the wrapped FormatException/TypeError is the only thing left to read. A self-signed certificate never produces DioExceptionType.badCertificate — dio raises that only with a validateCertificate callback — and a HandshakeException is a TlsException so it arrives as unknown. 403 is not a wrong address and has a case of its own, for the failed admin scan. Tests throw the real exceptions with a realistic content type, because a mock labelling a plain-text 401 as JSON tests a server that does not exist.

nodes.label: Library
nodes.rationale: A collection of series on the server, scanned from a folder and carrying a type. A library can be empty, which means the server has not scanned it yet. Avoid: collection, folder, shelf.
nodes.source_location: The server and what it holds

nodes.label: Library type
nodes.rationale: Which of Kavita's six kinds a library is (Manga, Comic, Book, Image, Light Novel, ComicVine). It decides what a series is made of and what every part of it is called, so it is never cosmetic. Avoid: format, genre, category.
nodes.source_location: The server and what it holds

nodes.label: Series
nodes.rationale: One work: a manga, a comic run, a book. The thing a cover in the grid stands for. Avoid: title, book, entry.
nodes.source_location: The server and what it holds

nodes.label: android.permission.INTERNET in the main manifest
nodes.rationale: Flutter's template declares INTERNET only in src/debug/ and src/profile/, so a release build shipped with no network at all and failed every request at the connection — a symptom indistinguishable from a server that is down. Neither analyze nor any Dart test catches it, and CI had only ever produced debug APKs. CI now unzips the bundle and greps its manifest with grep -qa, since a bundle's manifest is protobuf and some greps call that binary and report no match.

nodes.label: Cleartext HTTP permitted on both platforms
nodes.norm_label: cleartext http permitted on both platforms
nodes.rationale: A self-hosted Kavita is usually a bare IP on the LAN with no certificate. Neither config could be narrower: Android's only permits cleartext for hosts written down at build time, which a client of a user-named server cannot know, and iOS's narrower NSAllowsLocalNetworking has a scope Apple's own sources state inconsistently. Permitting cleartext is not the same decision as trusting a user-installed CA — Android's trust anchors stay system-only, so a self-signed HTTPS server is still refused. The login form validates the address itself because Uri.hasScheme is not enough: 'kavita.local:5000' parses with a scheme of 'kavita.local'.

nodes.label: An empty library is a state, not a blank screen
nodes.norm_label: an empty library is a state, not a blank screen
nodes.rationale: A library is empty because the server has not scanned it, so the copy points at the server and names the library — the name is picked out of the localized sentence by indexOf rather than concatenated, or a French sentence would be assembled in English word order. The dashed rounded outline (DashedBorderPainter) is the handoff's mark for a place to fill, as against solid borders that enclose something already there. Pullable, because after asking for a scan there has to be a way to look again.

nodes.label: Library scan is admin-only
nodes.rationale: POST /api/Library/scan?libraryId=N is behind Kavita's AdminPolicy (RequireRole Admin), and so is every other way in — scan-folder is [AllowAnonymous] but looks up the key's account and refuses a non-admin itself. There is no non-admin path, so the button is not drawn for one; a 403 is all it could earn. libraryId goes in the query string because the action takes a bare int. The scan is a background job: requested, never finished, by the call that returns 200. UserDto.isAdmin tests for 'Admin' and fails closed on a missing or malformed list, since guessing yes draws a button that can only fail; it is persisted on ServerEntry because a resumed session never logs in again, so it is as old as the last sign-in.

nodes.label: OfflineIndicator (status in the app bar)
nodes.rationale: A struck-through cloud in patraDanger on the trailing edge, not a banner over the content. A banner is a paragraph: it pushed the shelves down, said the same sentence on three screens at once, and was as loud on the twentieth glance as on the first. The sentence survives as the icon's tooltip (also its semantics label) and as a SnackBar on tap, because a struck-through cloud says nothing to a screen reader. Its test harness must build the client with overrideWith, not overrideWithValue: onReachabilityChanged is wired by the real provider, so a ready-made client leaves the indicator dead however unreachable the server is.

nodes.label: offlineProvider
nodes.rationale: Flips to true when a request fails to reach the server (dio connection/timeout errors) and back on the next success. Offline, unsaved chapters are dimmed and non-tappable and the reader falls back to the stored SavedChapter metadata so a saved chapter reads with no server at all.

nodes.label: Localization (en template, fr)
nodes.rationale: Never hardcode user-facing strings: add the key to both app_en.arb and app_fr.arb, run flutter gen-l10n, and use AppLocalizations.of(context) (non-nullable, configured in l10n.yaml). Generated files are committed. Widget tests run under en, and SectionLabel uppercases its text, so tests match 'CONTINUE'.

nodes.label: StatefulShellRoute navigation (four tabs)
nodes.rationale: /series/:id and /reader/:chapterId are declared outside the shell so they are full-screen. Use context.push() to drill down — it stacks the screen, giving the AppBar back arrow and correct Android back-button behaviour — and context.go() only for switching branch or login/logout redirects; using go for drill-down makes the system back button exit the app. The bottom bar measures its labels before showing them, because French labels are much longer than English ones and a large system font makes any of them overflow; PatraText.navLabel must stay the single definition of that style or the measurement is meaningless. Reading changes progress on the server, so a screen that pushed the reader invalidates its own provider when the push returns.

nodes.label: serverReachableProvider (GET /api/Health probe)
nodes.rationale: The settings server dot was a const patraOnline: green from the moment the screen was drawn with nothing behind it, and offlineProvider alone could not fix it because that flag only moves when a request fails. /api/Health is the right endpoint rather than a convenient GET: [AllowAnonymous], so it reports reachability even when the token has gone stale, and [SkipDeviceTracking], so polling does not churn the ClientDevice entry. Being offline outranks a probe that once succeeded, and the probe re-runs on foreground because the four tabs live in an IndexedStack and the card is never rebuilt from scratch. The state is said in words as well as colour — an 8pt dot that only changes hue is no indicator to someone who cannot tell those hues apart — and the dot's Semantics merges into the card's node for one screen-reader stop.

nodes.label: The fixed French glossary
nodes.rationale: Not a translator's choice: it matches what Kavita itself says in French, and test/entity_naming_test.dart fails if it drifts. volume=tome, chapter=chapitre, issue=numéro (with #), book=livre, specials=hors-série, storyline=arc narratif.

nodes.label: Offline
nodes.rationale: The state of not being able to reach the server. A property of the app's last attempt, not of the device's radio. Avoid: disconnected, no network.

nodes.label: localeProvider — forcing the language from Settings
nodes.norm_label: localeprovider — forcing the language from settings
nodes.rationale: 'Follow the device' is a value rather than the absence of one: localeProvider holds a Locale? and null is exactly what MaterialApp's locale takes to mean 'resolve against the system', so the default needs no separate representation. Restored before runApp like every other preference, and a stored code the build no longer ships resolves back to the device rather than to a language with no translations behind it. The picker is built from supportedLocales so a new translation appears by existing; the one manual step is a line in languageEndonym, because a language is listed under its own name and never translated — someone who has landed in a language they cannot read must be able to find their way out.

nodes.label: kavitaClientProvider
nodes.rationale: Watches only the session's identity (baseUrl, apiKey), not its tokens: the client patches its own tokens on refresh, so rebuilding it there would invalidate every data provider mid-read. It keeps the previous client alive across a logout, because screens can rebuild once more while the router redirects.

nodes.label: AuthState / ServerEntry (several servers, one session)
nodes.rationale: ServerEntry is a remembered server (baseUrl, username, tokens — never a password); an empty token means 'remembered but signed out'. AuthState is the list plus activeUrl, and AuthState.active is non-null only when the active entry still has tokens. main() loads it from flutter_secure_storage before runApp and injects it via initialAuthStateProvider; SessionStorage.load() still migrates the old single-server key layout. signOut keeps the entry but drops its tokens; switchServer keeps them so returning is one tap.

nodes.label: Login result
nodes.rationale: What a server answers a sign-in with: who you are and the tokens to be you. It is not a session — a session is a server entry that holds tokens, and this is only what one is built from. Avoid: user, session, credentials (those are what is sent, not what comes back).
nodes.source_location: The server and what it holds

nodes.label: Server entry
nodes.rationale: A Kavita address connected to at least once, remembered along with its tokens but never its password. Several can be remembered at once. Avoid: account, connection, instance.
nodes.source_location: The server and what it holds

nodes.label: Session
nodes.rationale: A server entry that currently holds tokens. Exactly one server entry can be the active session. Avoid: login.
nodes.source_location: The server and what it holds

nodes.label: mockSecureStorage() in test_support.dart
nodes.rationale: On a test binding flutter_secure_storage has no platform behind it and the Linux implementation reaches for libsecret, which never answers — so a write hangs the test rather than failing it, which reads as a stuck suite rather than a missing mock.

nodes.label: serverRetry on every networked provider
nodes.rationale: Riverpod 3 retries a failed provider with exponential backoff and no ceiling — right for a blip, wrong for being offline. Offline, the three home providers made 3 requests then 33 within the minute and kept going; each attempt drops the provider to AsyncLoading, remounting the Skeleton's repeating AnimationController and redrawing at ~89fps forever on a screen showing nothing. serverRetry bounds it to three attempts inside ~600ms and makes coming back online the user's move. kavitaClientProvider keeps its own retry => null because its StateError is control flow, not a failure. test/offline_retry_test.dart counts requests across a simulated minute — a test asserting only 'an error is shown' would have passed throughout.

nodes.label: magnify_gesture.dart (one-finger magnify)
nodes.rationale: Off by default. Pinching needs a second hand, which a person reading on a phone does not have. The artwork under the finger is carried towards it — one rule, not four cases, and there must never be an if (dy > 0) in that file; drag length sets the magnification (2.5x over 400pt) and letting go returns the page. At an edge the border is held and the grip gives way, which at these settings is the normal case, so what is pinned is where the view lands, not that a point stays under the fingertip. That only holds because the reference point is clamped to within travel/(maxScale-1) of the screen's middle (_band, ~267pt); outside it the page grows faster than the glue can carry it and pulling down walked the view down the page by ~1.6%. H and V cancel out of the derivation, so one number covers both axes. The anchor is the axis that has to be exhaustive in tests. Travel is absolute, not a fraction of the screen — the ruler is a thumb. The page-turn swipe is gone while the mode is on (two recognisers cannot share one drag) and vertical scrolling is excluded. The reference point comes from the pointer-down, never onPanStart, which reports ~18pt into the drag. drawnContent holds the artwork, not the canvas, against the edges.

nodes.label: ReadingDirection (one setting, three values)
nodes.rationale: Left-to-right, right-to-left, or vertical scrolling — the third is a direction, not a separate mode, and there is a single control for it. 'Webtoon' is Kavita's word, after the genre, and is gone from this app in code as well as on screen: what varies is the motion, not what is being read. It is verticalScroll rather than vertical because Kavita has two vertical readers (UpDown pages, Webtoon scrolls) and only the second is ours. Never write LTR/RTL in UI copy. The enum name is the persisted preference and an unrecognised string falls back to left-to-right silently, so _legacyNames still reads the stored 'webtoon' — renaming a value without that is how a setting resets itself on someone's device and says nothing.

nodes.label: Magnifying
nodes.rationale: The reading gesture in which a one-finger drag enlarges the page around the point pressed, as an alternative to pinching, which needs a second hand. Held rather than switched on: the page returns when the finger lifts. Off unless asked for, because it takes the swipe that turns a page. Avoid: loupe (a loupe is a lens over one region; this scales the whole page — the word named a rejected alternative and stuck to the accepted one), zoom mode, pinch, magnifier.

nodes.label: Reading direction
nodes.rationale: Which way the reader advances through a chapter: left-to-right, right-to-left, or vertical scrolling. One setting with three values — the third is a direction like the other two, not a separate mode sitting beside them. Avoid: mode, layout, LTR/RTL in anything a user reads.

nodes.label: Vertical scrolling
nodes.rationale: The reading direction in which pages run as one continuous strip and are scrolled rather than turned. Kavita calls it webtoon after the genre it was built for and separately offers a paged vertical direction we do not — which is why the word is 'scrolling' and not merely 'vertical'. On screen the one word 'Vertical' is enough while it is the only vertical direction in the picker. Avoid: webtoon, vertical mode, continuous mode, long strip.

nodes.label: Reader settings sheet (one cog, not a control per setting)
nodes.norm_label: reader settings sheet (one cog, not a control per setting)
nodes.rationale: The direction pill was right while direction was the only thing to say. Magnifying cannot be drawn as an icon the way a direction can, and a second pill would eat the chapter title inside a 56pt bar. The cog costs no extra tap, since the pill was a menu opener rather than a toggle. It is a sheet and not a PopupMenuButton because a PopupMenuItem pops its route when tapped and a switch inside one would dismiss the menu as it was flipped; ReadingDirectionRows is shared with Settings so the wording cannot drift. The two rows deliberately differ: picking a direction closes the sheet and overrides only this chapter, while the magnify switch leaves the sheet open and writes the preference through. Reading vertically the gesture is inert and the row says so, but stays switchable, because a direction belongs to the book and this belongs to the hand.

nodes.label: _VerticalScrollViewState placement guard
nodes.rationale: A scroll view has no initialPage, so it opens at offset 0 while the reader is on page 40; the first flick would report page 0 and post it back, wiping the place the chapter was opened at. It jumps after the first layout (offsets need the width) and _placed gags _onScroll until then. GET /api/Reader/chapter-info returns pageDimensions, which this view uses to lay pages out — and so keep the slider in sync — before any image has loaded.

nodes.label: ThumbStrip (accordion scrubber drawn at a computed offset)
nodes.norm_label: thumbstrip (accordion scrubber drawn at a computed offset)
nodes.rationale: An accordion keyed to the page being read: current widest, its two neighbours halfway, the rest at base size, so item extents are not uniform. The strip does not centre the current page — the bulge travels on the same linear law as the slider handle, because the two sit one above the other. The slider's padding comes from the strip (ThumbStrip.sliderPadding), since Material insets a Slider's handle 26pt inside its box and the difference keeps the markers agreeing at the ends. Sizes are shares of the screen's shortest side, never points: _baseShare 0.174 and _currentShare 0.33, a third being as wide as it can be before the slider stops reading as a slider; a tablet takes _tabletShareFactor 0.64 of that share rather than a bigger thumbnail. The one limit in points is a gesture — _heightBudget keeps the chrome short of the middle third, where a tap would otherwise seek. The strip has no scroll position: _offset is a function of the accordion's two pages and its clock, because jumpTo calls markNeedsLayout and the reader's tree is full of LayoutBuilders, so dirtying layout from inside layout killed the next frame. Sizes and offset are read from the same state in the same build; animated apart they measured 123pt of daylight. Nothing on the item-builder path may reach back into the reader — _thumbCacheWidth, _client and _savedChapter are resolved in didChangeDependencies or mirrored out of build.

nodes.label: ClientIdentity / ClientDevice headers
nodes.rationale: Kavita 0.9.1+ registers a ClientDevice per user from three headers, stamped by an interceptor rather than frozen into BaseOptions because one of them moves. X-Device-Id is a random per-install UUID in secure storage, without which Kavita's fallback fingerprint collapses every Android install into one device. The User-Agent is where Kavita reads the platform from (its parser greps for Android/iPhone/iPad/Mac OS, never 'iOS') and the only place the device model survives. X-Kavita-Client fills the device card and must match the web UI's regex exactly or the sender is still stamped Web App and loses everything else — hence the header is null until there is a screen to report. announceDevice renames the entry once per session to 'Patra on <device name>' and never touches a name the user typed in Kavita. appVersion is read off the binary via package_info_plus rather than compiled in, falling back to 0.0.0 — deliberately not a copy of the current version, since a hardcoded one is the string that drifts. The build number is deliberately not shown or carried.

nodes.label: Registered device
nodes.rationale: Kavita's own record of a client that has talked to it, one per installation, kept apart by an identifier this app generates and remembers. The server names it and the app renames its own entry once per session; it never touches a name a person typed in Kavita. Avoid: session, client, install.

nodes.label: Claude Design handoff as source of truth
nodes.norm_label: claude design handoff as source of truth
nodes.rationale: Kept at .claude/design/HANDOFF.md and untracked on purpose, so it is on this machine and absent from a fresh clone. Its §3 (direction pill) and §5 (retired unfinished-page mark) are superseded. Two hard rules: patraAccent (purple) = reading progress and identity, patraOffline (teal) = downloads and offline, never swapped; serif (Source Serif 4) only for titles of works, the wordmark, and reader page numerals. Never hardcode a color or a radius in a screen — lib/src/theme.dart holds every token.

nodes.label: System chrome comes and goes with the reader's own
nodes.norm_label: system chrome comes and goes with the reader's own
nodes.rationale: The chapter opens in SystemUiMode.immersiveSticky and returns to edgeToEdge when the centre tap raises the reader's bars, and again on the way out, so the clock is never over the page but is always one tap away. Every path that moves _showChrome goes through _showChromeAndBars or the two drift apart. iOS hides both for any fullscreen mode; Android honours it below API 36 and ignores it above (we target 36); an iPad in Split View keeps its status bar whatever the app asks.

nodes.label: isTabletLayout — three shapes, three answers
nodes.rationale: The handoff was drawn for a phone, so the iPad is ours to reason about. isTabletLayout asks the shortest side against tabletBreakpoint so a phone in landscape is still a phone. A column of rows runs the full width at the app's gutter — a capped 560 column left an 820pt iPad with 150pt of nothing down each side, and the answer to a tablet's width is a grid, not a narrower column. A grid of cards keeps card size and takes another column. A shelf and the reader canvas run edge to edge. Two things must never scale with the screen: a swipe pane (extentRatio derived from a width in points) and a button (capped at 280).

nodes.label: Android signing switch via android/key.properties
nodes.rationale: build.gradle.kts reads key.properties if present and falls back to the debug keys if not, so a fork and a fresh clone still build while Play — which refuses a debug-signed bundle — gets a real one. CI writes the file from secrets into the runner's temp directory and deletes it in an always() step. The artifact is an App Bundle (.aab), the only thing Play accepts. Losing the upload keystore is recoverable only if Play app signing is enabled.

nodes.label: Build number stays github.run_number
nodes.rationale: Both stores want a number that only ever goes up; a version read as a number would not clear run numbers already accepted (25 when the trigger changed) and would repeat on a second build of one version. run_number counts every run of this workflow file, pull requests included, so numbers jump between releases: increasing is the requirement, not consecutive. Renaming build.yml or its name: restarts the count at 1 and every upload after it is rejected.

nodes.label: iOS job's two signing paths
nodes.rationale: Chosen by whether this is a release ref AND the signing secrets exist, so a fork with no Apple credentials still builds green via the unsigned sideloadable IPA. Signing is written into ios/Flutter/Release.xcconfig — the baseConfigurationReference of the Runner target, not the project — because the same settings on xcodebuild's command line reach every target and the Swift Package Manager packages Flutter uses for plugins fail the archive with 'does not support provisioning profiles'. A target xcconfig also outranks the template's project-level development CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY that TestFlight rejects, and keeps the team ID in a secret. With DEVELOPMENT_TEAM present the flutter tool skips its hunt for a development certificate, which a runner holding only a distribution certificate can never satisfy.

nodes.label: Play internal-track upload as a third gated state
nodes.norm_label: play internal-track upload as a third gated state
nodes.rationale: Gated separately on PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON because the Play Developer API cannot create an application — the first bundle goes through the Console by hand — so the step stays skipped rather than red. tracks (plural) must never be omitted: the action's default is production. internal is chosen deliberately: no review delay, up to 100 testers, and it does not start the twelve-testers-for-fourteen-days clock that only a closed (alpha) test advances. The upload action is pinned to a commit, not a tag, because it is handed the service account key and a tag can be moved under it.

nodes.label: Releases are cut by a tag, not by a push
nodes.norm_label: releases are cut by a tag, not by a push
nodes.rationale: The tag is the version, not just the trigger: it is passed to --build-name, writing Android versionName and iOS CFBundleShortVersionString, so a shipped binary cannot disagree with the tag it was built from and nothing in the repository needs bumping. Push the one tag by name, never --tags, because GitHub creates no event at all for a push carrying more than three tags. Platform jobs decide the signed path from github.ref rather than the event name, so a workflow_dispatch aimed at a tag is the same release — the recovery hatch for a half-failed release, since GitHub's own re-run keeps its run number, which both stores reject as already seen.

nodes.label: SpreadLayout (two-page spreads and wide pages)
nodes.rationale: Which pages share a screen is SpreadLayout's call, not page ~/ 2: a scan that is itself a double page (Kavita's isWide, or dimensions plainly wider than tall — either is enough, since the server only flags files it measured) takes a screen of its own, because pairing it would shrink both pages to a quarter of the screen and run the spine through a drawing meant to be seen whole. A wide page shifts the parity of everything after it, so a step is a screen rather than a fixed number of pages, and the counter's span comes from the page arrived at. With no dimensions nothing is wide and the pairing is what it always was. The two pages of a pair are pushed together against the spine via Image.alignment, since centring each in its half joins them with a gutter that widens with the screen.

nodes.label: Spread
nodes.rationale: Two pages shown on one screen, in landscape. Which pages share a screen is a question about the pages, not arithmetic on the page number. Avoid: double page (that is a wide page), pair.

nodes.label: Wide page
nodes.rationale: A single page that is itself a double-page image. It takes a screen of its own and shifts the pairing of everything after it. Avoid: spread, landscape page.

nodes.label: _PagedView seek guard (_seeking, _reported)
nodes.rationale: A seek the reader asked for is not reported back to it: jumpToPage dispatches its scroll notification synchronously and PageView turns that into onPageChanged from inside the build that delivered the seek. In landscape the view reports the first page of the spread, so a seek to an odd page reports a page the reader did not ask for and setState runs mid-build; the frame then dies on 'Each child must be laid out exactly once' with a RenderErrorBox in _ScaffoldSlot.body. Any programmatic move of a PageController needs the same guard. Separately, _reported must be set in initState and not by a late initialiser: a late field runs at first read, which is the comparison in didUpdateWidget where widget.page is already the new page, so the guard skipped the jump — the first tap on a side zone moved the page number and left the pager, the second jumped two. It went unnoticed because a swipe takes the onPageChanged path.

nodes.label: The reader must never wrap itself in a LayoutBuilder
nodes.norm_label: the reader must never wrap itself in a layoutbuilder
nodes.rationale: OrientationBuilder is a LayoutBuilder, and the reader asked it a question it does not need layout to answer, since the body fills the window. A LayoutBuilder runs the builds of everything beneath it during layout — pages, tap zones, chrome, scrubber, every image frame and every Slider setState — and the screen died on debugNeedsLayout and _debugRelayoutBoundaryAlreadyMarkedNeedsLayout from scheduleLayoutCallback, then 'Each child must be laid out exactly once' with two _RenderLayoutBuilders in _ScaffoldSlot.body. Scaffold only wraps a body in its own LayoutBuilder with extendBody/extendBodyBehindAppBar set, so the duplicated child was ours, re-inflated under Scaffold's GlobalKey'd body. Read layout only where genuinely needed (the strip's width).

nodes.label: Icons come from gen_app_icons.sh, not flutter_launcher_icons
nodes.norm_label: icons come from gen_app_icons.sh, not flutter_launcher_icons

nodes.label: Kavita (the server)
nodes.rationale: The self-hosted server that owns the files, the metadata and the reading progress, and is the authority on all three. Almost every noun in the domain is Kavita's, because a client that renames the server's concepts ends up speaking a different language from the thing it browses. Avoid: the backend, the API, the remote.

nodes.label: Patra (Flutter Kavita client)
nodes.rationale: A Flutter mobile client (iOS + iPadOS + Android) for Kavita, a self-hosted manga/comics/book server. Linux desktop is enabled purely as a fast local dev target, not a shipping platform. EPUB reading is deliberately still on the roadmap.
